title: OpenChamber extensions
excerpt: Four panels for the OpenChamber rail: manage OpenCode agents, skills and MCP servers, and run a Pomodoro timer, without leaving the browser.
challenge: Managing OpenCode agents, skills and MCP servers means editing files by hand, remembering their keys and switching between terminal and editor. There is no central view or quick switch to turn each one on or off.
solution:
Four OpenChamber extensions, each a panel on the rail. Three edit the plain files OpenCode already reads, in place and in the same format. The fourth is a focus timer.

Agents panel
List, turn on, turn off, edit, and create OpenCode agents. Agents remain plain markdown files.
[https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-agents](https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-agents)

Global lists ~/.config/opencode/agents and the agent/ folder; Project lists .opencode/agents of the open project. Each row shows name, mode, description and model.

A switch turns an agent off (disable: true in the frontmatter) or on (the key is removed). The change is immediate and reverts only if the write fails.

Click a row to edit name (new agents), description, mode, model, temperature, instructions and tool permissions (Inherit, Allow, Ask or Deny, per tool and per MCP server). Rules not listed, such as bash and write, stay as written.

New checks the name and that the file does not exist. Delete takes two clicks. Search filters by name, description and model. Changes land in new sessions.

Built-in agents and those declared in opencode.json are not files, so they are not listed. A file with the same name shadows a built-in.

Skills panel
Hide skills from the model, show them again, edit, and create new ones. Skills remain SKILL.md files.
[https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-skills](https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-skills)

Global lists ~/.config/opencode/skills, ~/.claude/skills and ~/.agents/skills; Project lists the same folders of the open project. Each row shows name, description and path, with a badge for compatibility folders.

The switch writes disable-model-invocation: true to hide a skill; on removes it. A hidden row is dimmed with Off: the model does not offer it, but it stays loadable with @id.

Click to edit the ID (new skills), display name, description and instructions. Save applies.

Checks run as you type: no description or duplicate ID (error); over 500 characters, overridden by another folder, no instructions or frontmatter, description without when-to-use (warning); ID not kebab-case, name differs from ID, or hidden (info).

New creates a folder with SKILL.md or a single <id>.md file. Delete takes two clicks and removes a folder skill with its scripts and references. Search filters by name, ID and description. Changes land in new sessions.

Built-in skills, skills declared in opencode.json or HTTP catalogs, and skills hidden by permissions are not visible. If metadata sets opencode/autoinvoke: false, it wins; the panel reports it and leaves both settings.

MCP panel
See the MCP servers OpenCode has configured, which are on, and their full configuration. Remove them when needed. Servers stay in opencode.json.
[https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-mcps](https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-mcps)

Global reads ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json(c); Project reads opencode.json(c) and .opencode/opencode.json(c) of the open project. Each row shows name, local or remote, URL or command, and file and line.

The switch writes "disabled": true to keep a server from connecting; on removes the key. The entry stays as it is, and OpenCode picks up the change without a restart.

Click a row for the full detail, with the entry exactly as written. Credential-looking headers and environment values are masked, with Reveal; {env:NAME} never is.

Errors cover a server with no usable type, URL or command. Warnings cover credentials in the file or sent over plain http://, $VAR instead of {env:VAR}, and V1 placement or timeouts. Info covers unknown keys and servers that are off.

Delete takes two clicks and removes only that entry. Search filters by name, URL and command. Reload re-reads the files. The panel makes no network calls; it only reads and writes those config files.

Pomodoro panel
A focus timer: pick a type or make your own, and run it round by round, work then rest. A compact version sits in the Work Status section, with the clock and a pause button.
[https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-pomodoro](https://github.com/N4N1T0/openchamber-pomodoro)

Three types from Pomodoro Warrior: Classic Dungeon (25/5, 4 rounds), Siege Crypt (50/10, 2) and Lightning Raid (15/3, 6). Add your own with a name, work and rest minutes, and rounds. Start, pause, skip and reset; the round list shows where you are.

The run is saved as an end time, so reloading or switching away picks it up at the right moment. A toast and a beep mark each phase. Alerts only reach you while OpenChamber is open.

Installation
Install each extension separately: Settings → Extensions in OpenChamber, paste the repository URL, approve file access. Delete in agents and skills needs a local service until it is approved. Skills and MCPs are tagged: add #v1.0.0 to the URL to pin a version.

What they do not do
- they do not list built-in agents or skills, nor those declared in opencode.json
- the MCP panel shows configuration, not connection state; check that with opencode mcp list or /mcps
- switching off is not disconnecting: a running session keeps its tools
- adding a server is not in the panel (opencode mcp add); deleting an entry leaves OAuth credentials (opencode mcp logout <name>)
- permissions are not edited here
- the timer has no long break yet
- VS Code and the phone do not load extensions

Development
Each repository uses Bun. Built .js files are committed, so rebuild and commit after every source change; CI fails otherwise.
